 Hillel encourages interfaith early voting, student speakers
 Members of various religious communities gathered at Library Mall to reflect on the importance of voting and connection between religion Oct. 27
 By Lilly Nicandri 
 November 5, 2026 | 3:00am CST 
 University of Wisconsin Hillel hosted an event to encourage early voting, interfaith support and communication Oct. 27 on Library Mall.
 During the event student speakers reflected on the importance of civic engagement, then led students to the polls at Memorial Union and finished with a dinner at Hillel. 
 Student speakers highlighted the importance of building bridges between different faiths, voting for those who cannot be heard and emphasized every vote matters especially in an increasingly divided social environment. 
 Aaron Seligman, director of Community Relations at University of Wisconsin Hillel, told The Daily Cardinal there is often a stigma surrounding the combination of politics and religion.
 “I think people have this perception that you shouldn't talk about politics, you shouldn't talk about religion, it's too divisive, it's too controversial,” Seligman said. “I think it's important for students, particularly in an era where there’s cancel culture and social media, to actually come together in person and be proud of their whole identity.”
 Seligman went on to say religious voters are often associated with divisive social issues, and are not recognized for their broader religious and political beliefs that are often interconnected. 
 “We are voters, and our values are informed by our faith…We don't like to separate one identity from the other,” Seligman said.
 Seligman said he wanted the event to deter from the negative attention religious groups may encounter and focus on reaching out and building a positive space to celebrate all faiths and their impact in the broader campus voting community.
 One of the student speakers, Victor Margulius, representing the Orthodox Christian Student Club on campus, spoke about how his Orthodox faith impacts his voting practices.
 “Our church encourages us to take part in democratic life as a way of loving our neighbors,” Margulius said. “The point isn't to win for one side, it's for the people around us that matter that you vote…Eating with people who believe and vote differently is democracy at a human scale.” 
 Rhys McVann-Henkelmann, the advocacy coordinator at The Crossing , spoke next. The Crossing is a student community on campus that encourages the exploration of faith and advocates for human rights. 
 McVann-Henklemann said he isn’t religious, and shared a story about trying to pass a bill to protect women experiencing domestic violence. He said it was a strenuous process, and he talked to both political parties, but the bill didn’t pass. He said one representative said yes because of a promise she made to a young woman who survived domestic violence.

 “I think, more than partisanship sometimes, that it is the people that we elect into those offices, regardless of their political party, that determine which issues get heard and which issues get ignored,” McVann-Henkelmann said. “We should think about the people…that can't be heard, like that young woman, or the disenfranchised, or the hungry, or the poor who don't have the level of political power and leverage that we do today.”
 Speaker Elyse Weiner represented Hillel and shared a Jewish folk tale she said illustrated her beliefs on civic engagement and its relation to her religion. 
 “We're all on one ship together, and we all have to work together to keep it afloat,” Weiner said. “These Jewish stories have always taught me to look further than just myself and consider the needs of the community around me and the sense of responsibility doesn't stop at the Jewish community, but extends to everyone.”
 Weiner also spoke about standing against the bystander effect.
 “The bystander effect shows up in voting: ‘Oh, there are already enough people voting. My vote doesn't matter,’” Weiner said. “All of our faiths have taught us that every vote matters.”
 According to Weiner, college students have a big impact on the election outcomes in Wisconsin, and local and state elections are just as important as national elections.
 Dawn Drake, a student speaker representing the Pres House , a ministry of the Presbyterian Church focusing on providing a spiritual home for students, spoke about the importance of this event in an email to the Cardinal. 
 “As politics and religion grow increasingly polarized in the United States, creating opportunities for connection across those divides is especially important,” Drake said. “While people from different faith traditions may approach the world in different ways, many share a common commitment to contributing to the common good. Civic engagement offers a point of connection from which those connections can be built.” 
 Madeline Stephanie, a UW-Madison student and member of the St. Francis congregation, said she believes there should be more spaces where people can look for support regardless of their political or religious background. 
 “I think that as we become increasingly divided both religiously and politically, we need more spaces where we can really come together, free of judgment to interact,” Stephanie said. 
 Stephanie went on to speak about how her Christian faith has impacted how she votes and builds community. 
 “I grew up in an area where being Christian very much meant building community, but I think that also translates to a lot of other religious practices as well,” Stephanie said. “[Religion] changes the way that I vote and that changes the way I interact with others. I want to make sure all my actions are representative of building [a] community and providing support for other people.”
